item.title: Federal surplus 2026: +800 million
item.description: The Confederation expects a surplus of just under CHF 800 million for 2026, against the budgeted deficit of CHF 700 million. The improvement is due to the increase in income tax of 1.4 billion.
item.content:encoded:

item.title: Electric vans compared to traditional vans: new from 1 October 2026
item.description: The Federal Council will equate electric commercial vehicles up to 4.25 tonnes with traditional vans from 1 October 2026. Driving at 120 km/h on the motorway, national tachograph exemption: everything you need to know.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Federal Council equates electric vans with traditional vans from 1 October 2026 - Driving at 120 km/h on the motorway, national tachograph exemption - Five amended ordinances; cantons adjust by 1 February 2028
## Key facts - **What**: Regulatory equivalence of electric commercial vehicles ≤4.25 tons to traditional vans - When: Decision 19 August 2026; entry into force 1 October 2026 - Where: Switzerland (federal road traffic ordinances) - Who: Federal Council, after consultation - Adjustment deadline: 1 February 2028 for the cantons - Highway speed: 120 km/h for equivalent vehicles
The Federal Council announced on 19 August 2026 a decision destined to revolutionise the wheeled delivery industry in Switzerland. Electric commercial vehicles up to 4.25 tons will receive the same regulatory treatment as traditional vans, breaking down a series of administrative constraints that until now hindered the competitiveness of green mobility in national freight transport.
The decision stems from the examination of the results of the consultation and involves the amendment of as many as five federal ordinances on road traffic. The stated objective is twofold: to pave the way for the spread of electric mobility in the sector and to accelerate the decarbonisation of the delivery sector, a strategic priority for the Confederation in the framework of the transition ### Economic impact on national logistics
Equalization represents a concrete economic catalyst for delivery companies evaluating investments in electric fleets. Until now, a 4-tonne electric van remained subject to heavy vehicle rules: mandatory tachograph, motorway speed restrictions, and driving time constraints. These administrative burdens eroded the margins of ecological and economic advantage compared to traditional combustion models, discouraging the transition even for companies sensitive to sustainability.
With the new legislation entering into force on October 1, 2026, the calculation of operating costs changes radically. A driver of an equalized electric van will be able to:
- Save travel time on long motorway stretches, thanks to the permitted 120 km/h (vs. 100 km/h for traditional heavy vans) - Avoid daily tachograph completion and associated administrative compliance costs - Benefit from less frequent technical maintenance cycles, shortening vehicle downtime - Operate with greater schedule flexibility, thanks to exemptions from work and rest time constraints
These considerations directly affect the profitability of delivery services, especially for couriers and small [logistics companies](nav:companies) operating on repeated national routes (e.g., same-day deliveries from a distribution center to distant cities). Electric mobility thus becomes not only an environmental choice, but an economically rational one for the company budget.
### Job opportunities and cantonal adjustments
Transitioning to equalized vans will create new [opportunities in the logistics sector](nav:jobs) for drivers specialized in managing electric vehicles. The cantons have a window until February 1, 2028, to align their administrations and control systems with the new federal legislation. This deadline is crucial: it allows the Confederation to coordinate implementation nationwide, while cantonal authorities are expected to update registration procedures, technical inspections, and compliance checks.
Differences between cantons could still persist regarding motor vehicle tax costs or inspection methods, but operational rules will be uniform by February 2028. The national delivery and freight transport sector can therefore count on a homogeneous framework, which will be followed by a phase of operational stabilization during 2028.
## Useful tools for your case To verify your within/over 20 km tax scenario, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [tax return guide](nav:tax-return). ### Implementation Timeline and Practical Adjustments
The chronology is precisely defined by the Federal Council: October 1, 2026, is the effective date of the new equivalency. Drivers and companies intending to benefit must plan the purchase of electric vehicles up to 4.25 tonnes in view of that date. Until then, current rules remain in force (mandatory tachograph, speed limits, restrictions on driving times for vehicles over 3.5 tonnes).
From October 1, 2026 onwards, new electric vans registered under this threshold will be able to operate according to the new rules from the day they are entered in the vehicle registry. Vehicles already in circulation can be updated to the new operating procedures even after entry into force, provided they meet the technical equivalency requirements (weight up to 4.25 tonnes, electric propulsion, compliance with amended ordinances).
### Adjustment Procedures for Cantons and Administrative Management
The cantons must officially communicate transition procedures to industry operators by February 2028, particularly regarding: - Technical reclassification procedures for already registered vehicles - Criteria for verifying weight and actual configuration - Any local differences in the calculation of cantonal vehicle taxes - Timelines for upgrading IT control systems
This federal-cantonal alignment ensures that implementation takes place in a coordinated manner, reducing regulatory confusion across the various cantons and allowing companies to plan investments with certainty.
### Economic Evaluation and Use of Calculators
Those operating in the logistics and freight transport sector in Switzerland should monitor official announcements from their registration cantons starting in September 2026, to understand exactly how local registration and control systems will adapt to the new regulations. To evaluate the economic opportunity of investing in electric vans, it is useful to compare current operating costs with post-October 2026 projections, considering savings on fuel, maintenance, and travel times. With the [operating costs and tax analysis calculator](nav:calculator) you can estimate the monthly savings resulting from reduced travel times, lower maintenance costs, and the tax advantages of the ecological transition.

item.title: Sick pay: the system works well
item.description: Federal Council confirms: the system of protection for workers in the event of illness is adequate. Coverage at 85-90% in companies, only 0.13% of workers excluded.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Federal Council: sickness allowance system is adequate, no changes necessary - Coverage >85% for companies with 3+ employees, 90% for >50 employees - Only 0.13% of workers lack protection, mainly in micro-enterprises
## Key facts - **What**: Federal Council approves report on daily sickness allowances - When: August 19, 2026 - Where: Switzerland (federal decision) - Who: Federal Council and the Social Security and Health Committee of the Council of States - Coverage: 85% of companies with 3+ employees, 90% with 50+ employees - Excluded: 0.13% of Swiss employees
Bern, August 19. The Federal Council has approved the report in response to postulate 24.3465 from the Social Security and Health Committee of the Council of States, concluding that the current daily sickness allowance system is sufficient and does not require substantial changes.
The investigation examines the coverage rate of daily allowance insurance—the protection that ensures employees maintain their salary when they fall ill. The results show that the situation in Switzerland is overall positive. Coverage exceeds 85 percent for companies with at least three employees and reaches 90 percent for those with more than 50 employees.
### Marginal exclusions
Exclusions remain limited. Only about 0.5 percent of companies have not taken out any insurance, in most cases because they were refused admission or no offer was available. This affects approximately 0.13 percent of employees in Switzerland, primarily those employed in micro-enterprises with one or two people. Even in this fragile segment, 44 percent of workers are protected through a policy.
The vast majority of companies that have not subscribed to daily allowance insurance have internal regulations to guarantee salaries in the event of illness. The functioning of these mechanisms is [comparable to formal insurance](nav:health), offering similar protection to employees. Given these results, the Federal Council judges that local adjustments to the current rules are sufficient to address the few access difficulties encountered. A global reorganization of the system is not considered necessary, nor is the introduction of a general insurance obligation for all companies regardless of their size. The Federal Council report photographs a protection system that works for the vast majority of Swiss workers. But photography also reveals significant differences between large and small companies — a relevant element considering that small business is the backbone of the Swiss economy.
### Where coverage is strong, where it is weak
In medium and large companies, the system is consolidated. Above 50 employees, coverage reaches 90 percent, a rate that reflects stability and predictability. Even in the 3-49 employee bracket, 85 percent of covered companies report solid penetration. The market has developed competitive offers and insurance companies operate without too many obstacles.
The critical point emerges in microenterprises, those that employ one or two people. Here, 44 percent of the workforce is formally insured, while the rest is not. The known reasons are mainly two: sometimes insurers refuse to underwrite coverage on very small risk shares, or simply do not have an appropriate offer. Yet, even this criticality is mitigated by the fact that many microenterprise owners have internalized the principle of the wage guarantee in the event of illness, maintaining the salary to their collaborators through direct management, without formal insurance.

## In a nutshell - CET-N proposes to cancel changes to the Lex Koller of the last 40 years - Objective: to curb speculation and reduce land and property prices - The project aims to limit purchases by people residing abroad - Open discussion on stricter restrictions also for EU citizens and border crossers
## Key facts - **What**: Motion to strengthen Lex Koller (LAFE) - When: Proposal discussed by the CET-N, with review by the Federal Council - Where: Switzerland - Who: National Economic and Tax Commission (CET-N) - Amount: Over 1.5 million net immigration since 2002
The National Economic and Tax Commission (CET-N) has adopted a motion that marks a potential return to the past for the Swiss property market. The parliamentary act, promoted by National Councillor Thomas Aeschi (UDC/ZG), asks to annul all the changes made to the "Lex Koller" in the last fortyyears. The declared intention is to restore the regulatory situation prior to 1985, by acting on the federal law on the purchase of funds by people abroad (LAFE). The main reason given by the parliamentarian concerns the growing difficulties that middle-class families encounter in trying to buy a home. This criticality also involves small and medium-sized enterprises, often looking for suitable spaces for their operational activities.
According to the analysis proposed by Aeschi, The revision project of the 'Lex Koller' presented by the Federal Council outlines a significant change in the authorization regime for real estate purchases. The new provisions aim to specifically target foreign demand by introducing stricter constraints for commercial and residential properties. Regarding commercial real estate, residents abroad would no longer have the right to purchase them for rental purposes, being able to maintain the purchase without authorization only if intended for direct use in their own business. This measure directly affects the management of real estate assets by international entities.
### Impact on real estate and financial companies A further pillar of the crackdown concerns the general prohibition for foreigners to purchase listed shares of residential real estate companies. The restriction extends to regularly traded shares of real estate funds and SICAVs, financial instruments that have so far allowed foreign investors to access the Swiss market by bypassing the classic limitations of the law. Analyzing the positions that emerged during the consultation that ended in July, a clear divide is evident. While on one hand the SP and the SVP welcome the tightening, seeing it as a necessary bulwark to protect the purchasing power of tenants and those looking for homes, on the other hand, The Centre and real estate companies warn about the possible negative repercussions on the national economic system. The fear is that overly rigid regulation could slow down investments in an already complex sector.
The Swiss Group for Mountain Regions (SAB) has raised specific objections, arguing that such plans could damage the economy of alpine regions without providing a concrete solution to the housing shortage. According to the SAB and The Centre, the roots of the housing problem should not be sought exclusively in foreign demand, but rather in procedural delays and restrictive building regulations that hinder territorial planning. The divergence of views highlights how the issue of access to housing is closely linked to land management and urban densification policies. In this scenario of regulatory uncertainty, those planning investments or real estate purchases must carefully monitor parliamentary developments, as final decisions could significantly alter the requirements needed to operate in the Swiss real estate market, influencing both private individuals and industry professionals who need [information on the cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) to evaluate their investments.

Those who own real estate or intend to invest in real estate fund shares must be aware that the regulatory framework could undergo substantial changes in the near future. The current 'Lex Koller' rules remain in force, but the possible approval of the proposed restrictions would entail an adjustment obligation for those acting through corporate vehicles or investment funds.

item.description: 20-minute survey/Tamedia: 62% of Swiss against the neutrality initiative. But Ticino votes yes with 52%. Vote on 27 September 2026.

## In a nutshell - 20-minute survey/Tamedia of 12-13 August 2026: 62% of Swiss against the neutrality initiative - Ticino is the exception with 52% in favour, the only canton where initiative would pass - Feeding initiative rejected: 65% against, 31% in favour - Vote on September 27, 2026
## Key facts - **What**: Survey on two federal initiatives (neutrality and nutrition) - When: 12-13 August 2026 (detection), processing 13-17 August, vote 27 September 2026 - Where: German Switzerland, French Switzerland, Ticino - Who: 20 minutes/Tamedia, 13,154 participants - Neutrality results: 36% yes / 62% no; Power supply: 31% yes / 65% no
The first 20-minute survey/Tamedia on the two initiatives on the ballot on 27 September 2026 reveals a clear opposition of the Swiss population to both proposals. For the neutrality initiative, 62% are against the requested change, while only 36% support it. The remaining 2% remains undecided. The initiative on food has even less consensus: 31% in favour against 65% against, with 4% undecided.
But the most surprising fact concerns the regional differences. While German Switzerland and Romanian Switzerland clearly reject both initiatives, Ticino stands out from the rest of the country on the issue of neutrality: in our canton, the initiative would pass with 52% approval, against 45% against. It is a result at odds with the ### Ticino against the rest of Switzerland
The Ticino result on the neutrality initiative represents a resounding exception in the Swiss landscape. This gap highlights a Röstigraben that is not only linguistic but also political on a central issue for Switzerland. Proponents of the neutrality initiative argue that enshrining neutrality in the Constitution would prevent the Federal Council and politicians from weakening or interpreting it at their own discretion. They see a stricter constitutional wording as a guarantee against gradual changes in Swiss foreign policy.
Those who oppose the initiative, on the other hand, put forward arguments based on the Swiss tradition of openness and dialogue. According to the opponents, the initiative would severely limit Switzerland's ability to act in the face of global foreign policy challenges. Renouncing sanctions in the event of violations of international law could be seen as taking a stand in favor of aggressor states and damage Switzerland's reputation in the world. Finally, a rigid conception of neutrality would entail the sacrifice of cooperation in matters of security and defense, weakening the country's defensive capacity.
### Food supply: less divided, but still rejected
The food supply initiative shows a radically different situation. 65% of respondents oppose it, while 31% support the proposal and 4% remain undecided. Unlike the neutrality issue, no significant Röstigraben emerges: the entire national electorate moves with relative uniformity in its rejection. German-speaking Switzerland expresses 70% 'no' (27% 'yes'), French-speaking Switzerland 58% 'no' (37% 'yes'), and Ticino 50% 'no' (45% 'yes').
The only electorate that shows broad support is that of the Greens, with 69% in favor. The base of the PS appears divided instead: 46% support the initiative while 50% reject it. In all other parties, the opposition is marked: GLP (66%), SVP (74%), The Centre (75%), and FDP (83%). Gender and age also have an impact: the 'no' is more widespread among men (70%) than among women (59%), and retirees reach 74% in opposition.
### What proponents and opponents are asking for
Those who support the food supply initiative do not express a single dominant argument. 31% cite the possibility of achieving a higher degree of food self-sufficiency, thus reducing dependence on foreign countries in the event of a crisis — a legitimate concern considering how decisions on food affect the [cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living). 28% point instead to the protection of groundwater resources from pollution caused by fertilizers and pesticides. The main reason for opposition to the initiative, cited by 46% of opponents, concerns the 70% self-sufficiency target contained in the proposal. According to this criticism, the measure would end up turning into a 'state-imposed menu', leaving very little room for animal-based products and severely limiting consumer choices.
